blocks.html: In Reading Whole Words you learned to read a word sign by sign and stop at the determinative. Verbs read the same way. What is new in this course is what happens to a verb when it changes form, and that starts with its root.

An Egyptian verb is built on a root of consonants, usually two or three, sometimes four: sḏm "hear", ḏd "say", nḏm "be sweet". Every form of the verb keeps the root and adds endings, prefixes or a suffix pronoun.

Hieroglyphs write consonants, not vowels (Writing Without Vowels). Spoken Egyptian surely changed its vowels from one verb form to the next, the way English has sing, sang, sung. Those vowel changes are lost to us. What survives in writing is the root and the endings, so that is what we learn to read: the root tells you which verb it is, the endings tell you which form.

blocks.title: Two consonants or three?
blocks.q: How many consonants does the root of mn.n=sn have?
steps: Take off =sn "they" and the .n.

blocks.q: The verb ḏd "say" is written with the cobra and the hand. Read its root.
steps: The cobra (I10) is ḏ; the hand (D46) is d.
Neither is a complement here: each writes its own sound.
The root is ḏd.

blocks.html: Most verbs have three consonants (sḏm, ꜥnḫ "live", ḫpr "come into being"). A good number have two (ḏd, mn, rḫ "know"). A few have four or more, and some of those repeat two consonants, like nḏnḏ "consult".

Looking for vowels to tell forms apart. Students expect a past tense to look different the way "heard" differs from "hear". In writing, sḏm "hear" and sḏm "one who hears" can look exactly alike; the vowels that once separated them are gone. Tell forms apart by their endings and their place in the sentence. Check: cover the endings with your finger; what is left should be a root you can find in the dictionary.
Egyptologists pronounce roots with a helping e, sḏm "sedjem", ḏd "djed" (see Saying Words Aloud). That is a classroom convention, not the ancient sound.

blocks.html: Every verb has a root (Verb Roots). Grammars sort verbs into classes by the shape of that root, because the shape decides how the verb behaves in its forms.

The main classes: strong verbs, whose consonants all stay put (sḏm "hear"); third-weak verbs, ending in a weak j that usually drops (mrj "love", jrj "do"); second-geminate verbs, whose last two consonants are the same (mꜣꜣ "see"); causatives in s- (sꜥnḫ "make live"); and a handful of irregular verbs.

The weak consonants j and w were close to vowels. When a vowel or an ending stood next to them, they could vanish in speech, so the scribes stopped writing them. A doubled consonant behaves in a similar way: in some forms both consonants were heard and written, in others they merged into one. Strong consonants never disappear, so strong verbs look the same in every form.

Check: if a verb seems to have only two consonants and it is not in your list of two-consonant verbs, try adding a final j before you look it up.
Learn the class with the meaning when you learn a new verb, the way you learn a noun's gender. The next lessons on causatives and irregular verbs look at the last two groups more closely.

blocks.html: Some verbs are built from other verbs. The commonest way is to put s in front of a root. You met the result already: smn sits in many royal names, and sꜥnḫ in many epithets.
A causative is s- + a root, and it means "make (someone or something) do or be" what the root says: ꜥnḫ "live" → sꜥnḫ "make live, keep alive"; mn "remain, be firm" → smn "make firm, establish".

Many languages build causatives with a prefix or an ending (English has "en-" in enlarge, "make large"). In Egyptian the prefix is s. It turns an intransitive verb, one that takes no object, into a transitive one: you do not "live" something, but you can "make something live". That is why causatives so often have an object after them.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: sꜥnḫ "make live": the folded cloth s stands before the usual spelling of ꜥnḫ.

blocks.title: Make a causative
blocks.q: Write the causative of ḥtp "be content".
steps: Put s before the root: s + ḥtp.
sḥtp "make content, satisfy, pacify". Kings sḥtp the gods with offerings.

blocks.title: Read a causative
blocks.q: A text says sꜥnḫ=f rmṯ. What does it mean?
steps: sꜥnḫ is s + ꜥnḫ "live": "make live, give life to".
=f after the verb is its subject: "he".
rmṯ "people" is the object.

blocks.html: A causative belongs to the class of its root plus the s: smn behaves like a strong verb. In dictionaries causatives are listed under s, not under their root, so look up sꜥnḫ under s.

Causatives are common in royal and religious language, where kings and gods are the ones who make things happen: a king smn "establishes" monuments and laws, a god sꜥnḫ "keeps alive" the land, priests swꜥb "purify" a temple. When a verb you do not know begins with s, try reading the rest as a root you know before you reach for the dictionary.

Reading the s as a separate word. Students see s and think of the suffix pronoun =s "she" and read sꜥnḫ as "she lives". But a suffix pronoun comes after its word, never before it: "she lives" is ꜥnḫ=s. Check where the s stands: at the front, it is the causative prefix.

blocks.html: Most verbs follow the class rules of Verb Classes. A few very common verbs do not. Gardiner calls them anomalous; you will meet them on every page, so they are worth learning now.

The irregular verbs to know: rdj "give" (often written dj), jj or jw "come", and, with quirks of their own, jnj "bring" (stem jn) and wnn "be, exist" (stem wn). Their commands are special words: jmj "give!" and mj "come!".

These are the verbs people used most, and the most-used words in any language keep old irregular forms (think of English "be, am, was" or "go, went"). Egyptian rdj lost its r in speech in many forms, so the scribes often wrote only dj. The verb "come" had two stems, jj and jw, and different forms chose different ones.

blocks.html: Before learning the verb forms one by one, it helps to see the whole family. In Middle Egyptian I you read sentences with no verb at all (The Adverbial Sentence, The Nominal Sentence). Now the verb comes in.

Middle Egyptian has suffix forms (stem + subject: sḏm=f, sḏm.n=f, sḏm.tw=f), the stative (stem + its own endings: sḏm.kj), the infinitive (the verb as a noun), participles and relative forms (the verb as an adjective) and the imperative (commands). Grammars name every form after the model verb sḏm "hear".

blocks.html: Why name forms after sḏm? The grammarians needed a neutral label for a shape, not for a meaning, because the same shape can carry several meanings and the same English tense can come from several shapes. "The sḏm.n=f of jrj" means "the shape stem + .n + subject, made from jrj": jr.n=f.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The model form sḏm.n=f: the verb, the ending .n (water), the subject =f (horned viper).

blocks.title: Name the form
steps: The stem is ḏd "say".
Between the stem and the subject stands .tw.
That is the passive sḏm.tw=f: "she is told" or "it is said".

blocks.title: A form with no subject pronoun
steps: There is no = and no suffix pronoun.
The ending .kj belongs to the stative's own set of endings: "I".
So it is the stative: "I am alive".

blocks.html: Two more ideas run through the whole verb system. First, who does it: most forms carry their subject with them, as a suffix pronoun or a noun right after the verb, while the stative carries an ending and has its subject in front. Second, what the clause is doing in the sentence: the same sḏm=f can be a main statement, a wish, or a clause that depends on another verb. The lessons ahead take each form in turn, then show how clauses fit together.

Expecting English tenses. Students look for a past form, a present form and a future form. Egyptian forms tell you more about aspect (finished or ongoing) and about how the clause fits the sentence than about time. The sḏm=f can be a present, a wish or a future; the sḏm.n=f is usually past but can be "if he has heard". Check the context, and translate the time last.

blocks.html: Every verb has a noun form, the infinitive. English has two: "to hear" and "hearing". Egyptian has one, and its shape depends on the verb's class (Verb Classes).

Strong verbs show no ending in the infinitive: sḏm "to hear, hearing". Third-weak verbs drop their j and add -t: mrj → mrt "to love", jrj → jrt "to do". rdj also adds -t: rdjt (often written djt). Doubled verbs keep both consonants: mꜣꜣ "to see".

The infinitive is a noun, and nouns in Egyptian are masculine or feminine (Masculine and Feminine). The infinitives of strong verbs are masculine, with no ending. Those of the weak verbs are feminine and carry the -t, perhaps because a weak consonant at the end of the root was hard to keep: the -t gave the word a firm end.

blocks.title: Read it in a phrase
blocks.q: In r jrt mꜣꜥt "in order to do what is right", what is jrt?
steps: It stands after the preposition r, where a noun goes.
Its stem jr belongs to jrj "do"; the -t is the infinitive ending.

blocks.html: Reading the -t of jrt as a feminine noun "a doing" made from some other word, or as the eye jrt. The -t here is the regular infinitive ending of a third-weak verb. Check the context: after a preposition, or as the object of a verb, a verb stem with -t is almost always an infinitive.

The noun jrt "eye" is spelled with the same eye sign and t. Context separates them, and so does the stroke or determinative that "eye" usually takes. Egyptian writing is full of such look-alikes; reading the sentence, not the word alone, settles them.

blocks.html: The infinitive (Forms of the Infinitive) is a noun, so it goes wherever a noun can go. Three uses cover most of what you will read.

The infinitive is used (1) after prepositions: r sḏm "in order to hear", ḥr sḏm "hearing"; (2) as the object of another verb: wḏ.n ḥm=f rdjt ḥtp "His Majesty commanded the giving of an offering"; and (3) alone, in headings and captions: mꜣꜣ nṯr "Seeing the god".

A noun can follow a preposition, be the object of a verb, or stand alone as a label. An infinitive is the action itself, named as a thing. That is why English often needs "-ing" for it ("seeing the god") and only sometimes "to" ("in order to hear").

blocks.title: A caption
blocks.q: A tomb scene shows a man presenting food to a god. The caption reads rdjt ḥtp n nṯr. Translate it.
steps: rdjt is the infinitive of rdj "give" (with the -t of the weak verbs).
It stands alone at the head of the caption, naming the action.
ḥtp "an offering" is its object; n nṯr "to the god".

blocks.title: A famous title
blocks.q: The Book of the Dead calls its spells rꜣ n prt m hrw. What is prt?
steps: rꜣ "spell" (literally "mouth, utterance"), n "of, for".
prt is the infinitive of prj "go out", a third-weak verb, with its -t.
m hrw "by day".
blocks.a: The infinitive "going out": "Spell for going out by day".

blocks.html: When you meet a verb after a preposition, try both English renderings and keep the one that sounds natural. ḥr with an infinitive usually wants "-ing" ("saying"), r with an infinitive after a verb of motion usually wants "to" ("he came to hear"), and m with an infinitive of a verb of motion wants "-ing" again ("coming"). Each of these grows into a construction of its own later in the course.

Translating every infinitive as "to X". Captions and titles like "Hunting in the marshes" or "Seeing the god" use the infinitive as a plain noun, so English wants "-ing", not "to". Check: if "to" sounds odd in English, try "-ing" or "the …ing of".
The pseudoverbal construction, "he is hearing", is built from the first use, a preposition with an infinitive. You will meet it in The Pseudoverbal Construction.

blocks.html: An infinitive is a noun, and in Using Suffix Pronouns you learned that a suffix pronoun on a noun shows its owner: pr=f "his house". On an infinitive, the "owner" can be either the one who acts or the one acted on.

A noun or suffix right after an infinitive can be its subject or its object: m-ḫt jjt=f "after his coming" (=f does the coming), r mꜣꜣ=f "in order to see him" (=f is seen). If both are named, the object comes first and the doer follows with jn "by": rdjt ḥtp jn nsw "the giving of an offering by the king".

English does the same with nouns of action. "The king's praise" can be the praise the king gives or the praise he receives; only the sense tells. With an Egyptian infinitive, the verb helps you decide. An intransitive verb (jj "come", ꜥnḫ "live") has no object, so its suffix can only be the subject. A transitive verb (mꜣꜣ "see", rdj "give") usually has its object right after it.

blocks.title: An intransitive verb
steps: m-ḫt "after" is a compound preposition (Compound Prepositions).
jjt is the infinitive of jj "come", which takes no object.
So =f is the one who comes: "after his coming".

blocks.title: A transitive verb
steps: rdjt is the infinitive of rdj "give".
"Give" needs an object, and n=j "to me" names the receiver.
So =f is what is given: "giving it to me".

blocks.title: Doer and object both named
steps: sḏm is the infinitive, with its object mdt "the words".
jn "by" introduces the doer, zꜣ=f "his son".
blocks.a: "The hearing of the words by his son."

blocks.html: A practical order of questions helps. First, is the verb transitive? If not, the suffix is the subject. Second, if it is transitive, is a doer already named, in the main clause or after jn? Then the suffix is the object. Third, if neither settles it, read the sentence both ways and keep the one that fits the story. Egyptian writers relied on context here, and so do Egyptologists: translations of the same line sometimes differ for exactly this reason.

Always reading the suffix as the subject. Students carry over "his house" and read r mꜣꜣ=f as "in order that he see". With transitive verbs, the suffix is often the object. Check: does the verb take an object? Is a doer named elsewhere, in the main clause or after jn?

blocks.html: You know the suffix pronouns (Suffix Pronouns) and their uses on nouns and prepositions. Put one on a verb stem and you have the most common verb form of all, the sḏm=f.
The sḏm=f is the verb stem followed by its subject: sḏm=f "he hears", sḏm=s "she hears", sḏm=j "I hear". With a noun subject, the noun follows the verb: sḏm z "the man hears".

On a noun a suffix shows the owner; on a preposition, the object; on a verb, the doer. The pronoun is the same little word in all three places; its job comes from what it is attached to. So pr=f is "his house", n=f "to him", and sḏm=f "he hears". The grammarians named this whole family of forms the suffix conjugation, after the suffix that carries the subject.

blocks.html: Reading sḏm=f as "his hearing". The habit from nouns (pr=f "his house") is strong. But when the stem is a verb at the head of its clause, the suffix is the subject. (An infinitive with a suffix can mean "his hearing", as in the last lesson; it stands where a noun goes, after a preposition or another verb.) Check: is the word at the head of the clause? Then read the suffix as the doer.

blocks.html: The same shape works for every strong verb: rḫ=k "you know", ꜥnḫ=n "we live", sḥtp=sn "they satisfy". Learn the eight suffixes once and you can make the sḏm=f of any verb.

Egyptologists write the sḏm=f with an equals sign before the suffix, following the Leiden convention, and older books write a dot (sḏm.f). Either way, the answer boxes on this site accept sḏm=f, sḏm.f or sDm=f.

blocks.html: With a sḏm=f (The sḏm=f) the subject follows the verb. That one fact fixes the word order of the whole verbal sentence.

The word order of a verbal sentence is verb, subject, object, then adverbs and prepositional phrases: dj nsw ḥtp "the king gives an offering"; sḏm nsw ḫrw m pr "the king hears the voice in the house".

Because the subject is attached to the verb as a suffix in so many sentences, the verb is naturally first, the subject right behind it. A noun subject takes the same place, and the object follows the subject. Phrases saying where, when and how come last, as in The Adverbial Sentence. One wrinkle: a short dependent pronoun object jumps ahead of a noun subject, ḥz.n wj nsw "the king praised me".

blocks.cap: Verb, subject, object: sḏm "hears", nsw "the king", ḫrw "the voice".

blocks.title: Put the words in order
blocks.q: Write "The god knows the name" with rḫ "know", nṯr "god", rn "name".
steps: Verb first: rḫ.
Subject next: nṯr.
Object last: rn.

blocks.title: A familiar sentence
blocks.q: In the offering formula, dj=f prt-ḫrw follows the name of a god. Who gives what?
steps: dj is the verb "give" (a form of rdj).
=f "he", the god just named, is the subject.
prt-ḫrw "an invocation offering" is the object.
blocks.a: The god gives the invocation offering.

blocks.title: Where the phrase goes
blocks.q: Translate sḏm z mdt m njwt.
steps: Verb sḏm "hears", subject z "the man", object mdt "the words".
m njwt "in the town" comes last.
blocks.a: "The man hears the words in the town."

blocks.html: Putting the subject first, English style. nsw sḏm ḫrw does not mean "the king hears the voice" as a plain statement, and sḏm ḫrw nsw would make the voice the hearer. Check: the word right after the verb is its subject.

Reading a long sentence becomes much easier once you expect this order. Find the verb at the head, take the next noun or suffix as its subject, the next noun as its object, and leave the prepositional phrases for last. If a sentence seems to make no sense, check whether you have taken the object for the subject.

Some sentences do put a noun first, for emphasis or with particles like jw and mk before the stative (The Stative in Sentences). Those are different constructions, each with its own rule. In a plain sḏm=f sentence, the verb leads.

blocks.html: Knowing the shape of the sḏm=f (Noun Subjects and Word Order) is half the work. The other half is deciding what it means, and the sḏm=f means more than one thing.
The sḏm=f expresses general or present action ("he hears"), wishes ("may he hear"), and, after certain words, the future ("he will hear") or a condition ("if he hears"). Context decides which.

Behind the one written shape sḏm=f stood several spoken forms, with different vowels and sometimes a doubled consonant, as Gardiner already saw in the weak verbs (jrr=f beside jr=f). Those forms had different meanings. Since writing hid most of the differences, readers today rely on the words around the verb: a particle before it, the kind of text, the clause it belongs to.

blocks.html: In practice, read the sentence first as a plain present ("he hears"), then ask whether anything around the verb changes it. A particle or a formula usually settles the matter. When nothing does, the general present is the safest choice, and you can mark a future or a wish as a possibility in a note.

Giving every sḏm=f a present tense. "He gives an invocation offering" is a fair word-for-word reading of dj=f prt-ḫrw, but the formula is a prayer: "may he give". Check the setting before you choose the tense: a formula, a blessing, a particle like ḥꜣ or jr.
The sḏm=f also appears after the negative n, where it means "he did not hear" (Negation with n), and after rdj "cause" (rdj with the sḏm=f). These are learned as fixed patterns.

blocks.html: Strong verbs look the same in every sḏm=f. Weak and irregular verbs do not (Verb Classes, The Irregular Verbs). Here are the forms you will meet most.

In the sḏm=f, third-weak verbs usually drop the j: jr=f "he does", mr=f "he loves"; some forms double the second consonant instead, jrr=f. rdj usually appears as dj=f "he gives". Doubled verbs show mꜣꜣ=f "he sees" or, in some forms, mꜣ=f.

These changes come from speech. The weak j and the r of rdj faded when vowels moved around them, and scribes wrote what they heard. The doubled forms (jrr=f, mꜣꜣ=f) belong to a group of sḏm=f forms that Gardiner called imperfective; the shorter ones (jr=f, mꜣ=f) to the perfective. You do not need the theory to read: you need to know that jr, jrr, dj and mꜣ are forms of jrj, rdj and mꜣꜣ.

A doubled second consonant in a third-weak verb (jrr, mrr) is part of the form, not of the root, so take it off as well. The dictionary form is always the full root.

Missing jr=f because the j and r are written with one sign. Students look for a reed leaf j and a mouth r and find only an eye. blocks.html: rdj means "give" (The Irregular Verbs). Followed by another sḏm=f, it takes on a second meaning that you will see constantly in narrative.
rdj + a sḏm=f means "cause that …, let …": rdj.n=f sḏm=j "he let me hear, he caused me to hear". The command form jmj works the same way: jmj sḏm=f "let him hear!".

Think of "give" in English: "give him to understand" means "cause him to understand". Egyptian went further. What rdj "gives" here is a whole clause, sḏm=j "I hear", so "he gave that I hear" becomes "he let me hear". The second verb keeps its own subject, which is why the sentence has two suffix pronouns.

blocks.html: The pattern is very common in royal inscriptions and in biographies, where officials boast of what the king caused or allowed: rdj.n ḥm=f jj=j "His Majesty caused me to come", that is, he had me brought. In the offering formula, by contrast, dj=f prt-ḫrw is plain "may he give": there the next word is a noun, not a verb with its own subject. Watch what follows rdj: a noun means "give"; a verb with a subject means "cause" or "let".

blocks.html: Translating rdj as "give" here. "He gave, I heard" or "he gave my hearing" misses the construction. When rdj (or jmj) is followed directly by another verb with its own subject, read "cause" or "let". Check: count the subjects. Two verbs with two subjects in a row is the sign of this pattern.

blocks.html: The sḏm=f is stem + subject (The sḏm=f). Slip one more sign between them and you have the second great form of the suffix conjugation.

The sḏm.n=f is stem + .n + subject: sḏm.n=f "he heard", ḏd.n=j "I said", sḏm.n nsw "the king heard". Third-weak verbs use their short stem: jr.n=f "he did", mr.n=s "she loved"; rdj keeps its r: rdj.n=f "he gave".

The .n is an old ending, probably related to the preposition n long before Middle Egyptian, but in the classical language it is simply part of the verb form. What matters for reading is where it stands: between the verb stem and the subject, a place where no preposition could be, since a preposition needs a word after it to point to, and here the subject follows directly.

blocks.html: With a noun subject the form is just as regular: ḏd.n zꜣ=f "his son said", jj.n ḥm=f "His Majesty came". The .n sticks to the verb, and the noun follows as a separate word.

Reading the .n as the preposition n "to, for". Students turn sḏm.n=f into "he hears for him" or "hear for him". A preposition needs an object after it, and here the next word is the subject of the verb. Check where the n stands: right after the verb stem and before the subject, it is the .n of the sḏm.n=f. Note also jr.n=n "we did": the first n is the ending, the second the suffix "we".
When =n "we" follows the .n, scribes sometimes wrote the water sign only once. The context tells you whether "we did" or just "he did" is meant; transliterations restore both, jr.n=n.

blocks.html: You can build any sḏm.n=f now (The sḏm.n=f). Its meaning is more settled than that of the sḏm=f, but not quite the English past tense.

The sḏm.n=f expresses completed action. In a narrative it is usually a simple past ("he gave"); in speech it can be an English perfect ("he has given"); after jr "if" it is "if he has done". It is never a future.

A completed action is one seen as finished, whenever it happened. In a story about the past, finished actions are past events: "he came, he saw". In a speech, an action just finished is a perfect: "I have come to you". In a condition, the speaker imagines the action finished: "if you have heard". English splits these among three tenses; Egyptian uses one form for all of them.

blocks.html: The verb rḫ shows the idea of completion clearly. Its root means "come to know, learn", so rḫ.n=f "he has learned" amounts to "he knows". Several verbs of knowing and perceiving behave this way; when a past tense makes no sense, try the present state that results from the action.

So when you translate a sḏm.n=f, start with the simple past, then adjust. In a speech where someone reports what they have just done, "I have…" is often better. In a condition, "if… has…". With verbs like rḫ, a present. What you will not need is a future or a wish: those belong to other forms, above all the sḏm=f.

Giving the sḏm.n=f a future meaning after jr "if". English says "if you hear" about the future, so students write "if you will hear" for jr sḏm.n=k. The form still means completed action: "if you have heard". Check: put "have" into your English, then smooth it if the sentence allows.

blocks.html: In Middle Egyptian I you used jw before adverbial sentences (jw and mk). It also stands before verb forms, and its most common partner in biographies is the sḏm.n=f.
jw sḏm.n=f states a past event as a fact: jw jr.n=j mꜣꜥt "I did what is right"; jw rdj.n=j t n ḥqr "I gave bread to the hungry". The jw is not translated.

jw marks the clause after it as a statement in its own right, something the speaker sets down as so. A tomb owner telling his life does exactly that, line after line: I did this, I gave that. So jw + sḏm.n=f became the standard way to list deeds in autobiographies. English has no word for jw; the plain past tense already carries the sense of "this is what happened".

blocks.html: In narrative you will also meet other ways of moving a story along, such as ꜥḥꜥ.n + sḏm.n=f "then he did…" and the form sḏm.jn=f "then he heard" (as in ḏd.jn=f "then he said"). They work like jw + sḏm.n=f, with a sense of sequence. You will see them in Sinuhe and the Eloquent Peasant.

Because these lines repeat from tomb to tomb, learn them as phrases. Once you have read jw rdj.n=j t n ḥqr a few times you will see it at a glance, and the less familiar lines around it become easier, since they follow the same pattern: jw, a sḏm.n=f with =j, an object, and a phrase.

Reading jw as a separate verb "is" or as the verb "come". "It is that I did what is right" makes the sentence clumsy and changes nothing. Check: when jw stands before a sḏm.n=f, translate the sḏm.n=f alone as a past tense.

blocks.html: Every form so far carries its subject after the verb. The stative, which Gardiner calls the old perfective, is different: it has a set of endings of its own, and its subject, if named, stands before it.

The stative endings are: .kj (I), .tj (you, one person), .w or no ending (he), .tj (she), .wjn (we), .tjwnj (you, more than one), .w (they). Examples: jj.kj "I have come", jj.tj "she has come", jj.w "he has come".

The stative is the oldest verb form of Egyptian, and its endings are related to similar endings in other Afroasiatic languages (the family of What Egyptian Is). Because the endings already show the person, the stative does not need a suffix pronoun. In writing, the endings were often shortened or left out, especially .w, so transliterations sometimes restore them in brackets.

blocks.html: In hieroglyphs the endings are short: the basket k with a reed leaf or two strokes for "I", the bread loaf t with two strokes for "you" and "she", the quail chick w (often left out) for "he" and "they". Because they are small and often abbreviated, read them together with the subject before the verb: the subject usually tells you which person is meant.

Confusing the stative .tj with the feminine dual -tj (The Dual). Both are written with the bread loaf and two strokes. The dual ends a noun, nṯrtj "the two goddesses"; the stative ending sits on a verb that follows its subject, zꜣt=f jj.tj "his daughter has come". Check: is the word a noun or a verb, and does a subject stand before it?

blocks.html: You can recognize the stative by its endings (Stative Endings). What it means depends on the kind of verb.

The stative describes a state. With an intransitive verb it is the state the subject has reached: jw nsw jj.w "the king has come, the king is here". With a transitive verb it is the state of having been acted on, so it reads as a passive: jw pr ḫtm.w "the house is sealed".

Think of English "gone" and "sealed". "He is gone" describes where someone ended up after going; "the jar is sealed" describes the jar after someone sealed it. Egyptian has one form for both. An intransitive verb has only one participant, the subject, so its state is the subject's own. A transitive verb has a doer and a thing done to; its state belongs to the thing done to, which therefore becomes the subject.

blocks.html: A few verbs break the pattern. The most common is rḫ "know": its stative rḫ.kj means "I know", not "I am known", because knowing is a state the knower is in. Treat such verbs as exceptions to learn; the dictionary usually notes them.

Verbs of motion are the clearest intransitive cases. jj "come", šm "go", prj "go out" and ꜥq "enter" all have statives that say where someone now is: arrived, gone, out, inside. English often needs "is" or "has" for them: "he is gone", "she has arrived".

Translating a transitive stative as active. jw pr ḫtm.w is not "the house sealed" (as if the house did the sealing) but "the house is sealed". Check: if the verb normally takes an object, ask whether the subject could be the doer. If not, read the stative as a passive.

blocks.html: The stative has its endings (Stative Endings) and its meaning (What the Stative Means). Now, where does it stand in a sentence?

The stative follows its subject, like an adjective after a noun. The subject is a noun or a pronoun, often after jw or mk: mk wj jj.kj "look, I have come"; jw=f jj.w "he has come"; jw zꜣt=j ꜥḥꜥ.tj "my daughter is standing".

The stative describes its subject the way an adjective does, so it goes where a description goes, after the thing described. This is the same order as in the adverbial sentence, z m pr "the man is in the house": subject first, then what is said about it. Gardiner groups subject + stative with subject + ḥr + infinitive as one family, the pseudo-verbal construction (The Pseudoverbal Construction).

blocks.html: Both jj.n=f and jw=f jj.w can be translated "he came" or "he has come". They are not the same, and telling them apart sharpens your translation.

The sḏm.n=f reports an act, with its subject after the verb: jj.n=f "he came". The stative describes a state, with its subject before the verb: jw=f jj.w "he has come, he is here". Look at where the subject is and at the ending.

An act happens at a moment; a state lasts. jj.n=f tells that the coming took place. jw=f jj.w tells that he is now in the condition of having come, that is, present. With transitive verbs the difference is sharper still: ḫtm.n=f pr "he sealed the house" is an act with a doer; jw pr ḫtm.w "the house is sealed" describes the house, with no doer named at all.

blocks.html: Writers chose between the two with care. A tomb owner lists his deeds with jw + sḏm.n=f, as acts; a letter writer who says "look, I have arrived" uses the stative, because what matters is that he is there now. When you translate, keep the difference: "he came" for the act, "he is here" or "he has come" for the state.

Treating the two as interchangeable. Both may come out as "he has come" in a loose English version, but the Egyptian forms say different things. Check two things: is the subject before or after the verb, and is there a .n or a stative ending?

blocks.html: In Adjectives you learned that an adjective follows its noun and agrees with it: z nfr "a good man". A verb can do the same job. The form that lets it is the participle.

An active participle means "one who does": sḏm "one who hears", ḏd mꜣꜥt "one who speaks the truth", z sḏm ḫrw "the man who hears the voice". It follows its noun and agrees with it like an adjective, and it can take an object.

A participle is half verb and half adjective. As a verb it can have an object and adverbs: sḏm ḫrw m pr "who hears the voice in the house". As an adjective it describes a noun and takes the noun's gender and number. What it does not have is a subject of its own: the noun it describes is the one doing the action. That is the difference from a sḏm=f, which always names its subject after the verb.

blocks.html: Third-weak and doubled verbs have two kinds of participle. The imperfective doubles a consonant (mrr, jrr, mꜣꜣ) and suits repeated or lasting action: "one who loves". The perfective does not (mr, jr, mꜣ) and suits a single act: "one who loved". Strong verbs usually look the same in both, so let the sense guide you.

blocks.html: Reading a participle as a finite verb with a missing subject. Students turn z sḏm ḫrw into "the man hears the voice". That would be sḏm z ḫrw, verb first. Here the verb comes after the noun, describing it: "the man who hears". Check the order: a verb that follows a noun and has no subject of its own is a participle.

Participles are everywhere in titles and epithets, the phrases that describe officials and kings: "one who does what his lord praises", "who speaks and it happens". Learning to spot them makes those long strings of praise readable.

blocks.html: An active participle names the doer (Active Participles). A passive participle names the one the action is done to.

A passive participle means "one who is (or was) done to": mrj nb=f "beloved of his lord", ḥzj nb=f "praised by his lord", dj ꜥnḫ "given life". The noun right after it, if any, names the doer, as a direct genitive.

"Beloved of his lord" is a good model. The person described is loved; the one who loves comes after, as in the direct genitive, "of his lord". Egyptian builds many of its most common epithets this way, because they say how others regard someone: loved, praised, favored. In writing, active and passive participles often look alike; the meaning settles which is meant.

blocks.html: The forms are like those of the active participle. Third-weak verbs often show a j or a doubled j at the end of the perfective passive (mrj, ḥzj, sometimes written mrjj), and doubled forms for the imperfective (mrrw "one who is loved, always"). These are transliteration details; what you must decide when reading is who does the action.

You will meet these epithets after names on stelae and in tombs: an official is mrj nb=f and ḥzj nb=f, a king is mrj of a god and dj ꜥnḫ "given life". Read them as a set of polite descriptions rather than as statements, the way English uses "beloved" or "esteemed".

Making every participle active. "One who praises his lord" sounds fine in English, so students choose it for ḥzj nb=f. But the formula praises the official, not his loyalty to praise. Check: does the sentence make the person the doer or the receiver? If a noun after the participle could be the doer, the participle is probably passive.

blocks.html: Participles behave like adjectives (Active Participles), so they agree with the noun they describe, and like adjectives they can also stand alone as nouns.

A participle takes the ending of its noun: no ending for a masculine singular (z sḏm "a man who hears"), -t for a feminine (zꜣt sḏmt "a daughter who hears"), -w for a plural (nṯrw sḏmw "gods who hear"). Standing alone it is a noun: sḏmw "those who hear", sḏmt "she who hears".

This is the agreement you already know from adjectives: zꜣt nfrt "a good daughter". A participle is a verbal adjective, so it follows the same rule. Adjectives can stand for a person ("the good", "the great"), and so can participles; the ending then shows who is meant, one man, one woman, or several.

blocks.html: A participle describes a noun as the doer (Participles in Phrases). But what if the noun is the thing done, "the thing that he gave"? Then Egyptian uses a relative form.

A relative form is a verb form with its own subject that describes the noun before it: rn ḏd.n=f "the name that he said", pr jr.n=f "the house that he made". It agrees with that noun: after a feminine noun it takes -t before the .n: ḫt rdjt.n=f "the thing that he gave".

The relative form looks like a sḏm.n=f (stem + .n + subject), but it works like an adjective, the way a participle does, so it agrees with its noun. English needs a whole clause with "that" or "which" for it. The noun described is usually the object of the verb (what was said, made, given); the subject is the suffix or noun after .n.

blocks.html: Relative forms also exist from the sḏm=f, for present and general action: mrr=f "whom he loves". The one you will meet most in narratives and on monuments is the one from the sḏm.n=f. On family stelae it appears in ms.n and jr.n, "whom (the mother) bore" (Families on Stelae).

Compare the two kinds of verbal adjective. In z sḏm ḫrw "the man who hears the voice" the noun is the doer: a participle. In ḫrw sḏm.n=f "the voice that he heard" the noun is what is heard, and the doer is the suffix: a relative form.

Reading ḫt rdjt.n=f as two clauses, "the thing; he gave". The verb describes the noun before it, so read the pair as one phrase: "the thing that he gave". Check: if a noun is followed by a sḏm.n=f-like form and the sentence lacks a verb of its own, you have a relative form.

blocks.html: Participles and relative forms make relative clauses out of verbs. When the clause has no suitable verb, for example "the man who is in the house", Egyptian uses a little adjective, ntj, made from the genitive n the way the nisbes of Nisbe Adjectives are made.

ntj "who, which" introduces a relative clause and agrees with the noun it describes: ntj (masculine), ntt (feminine), ntjw (plural). z ntj m pr "the man who is in the house"; zꜣt ntt m njwt "the daughter who is in the town". Its negative is jwtj "who … not": z jwtj zꜣ=f "a man who has no son".

ntj is a nisbe adjective: "the one belonging to …". Like every adjective it takes the gender and number of its noun. What follows it is a full clause, often an adverbial phrase (m pr) but also a whole sentence with its own subject: zꜣt ntt jt=s m pr "the daughter whose father is in the house", literally "the daughter who her father (is) in the house".

blocks.html: Every suffix form so far has been active: "he hears", "he heard". To say "he is heard", Egyptian adds one more small ending.
Adding .tw between the stem and the subject makes a passive: sḏm.tw=f "he is heard"; with a noun, rdj.tw ḥtp "an offering is given". The subject of the passive is the one acted on.

.tw began as an indefinite pronoun, "one, someone": sḏm.tw "one hears". "One hears him" and "he is heard" say the same thing, and Egyptian came to treat the .tw form as a true passive, with the person acted on as its subject. That history explains why .tw can also appear with no subject at all: ḏd.tw "one says, it is said".

blocks.html: The passive often has no doer at all: that is one reason to use it. When the doer is named, Egyptian adds it with jn "by": sḏm.tw mdt jn nsw "the words are heard by the king". In practice, most passive sentences leave the doer out, and English translations often turn them back into actives with "one" or "they": "they say", "one hears".
In a dictionary, look up a passive under its verb: sḏm.tw under sḏm. The .tw is never part of the root.

Reading .tw as the dependent pronoun ṯw "you". The two are close, but ṯw is a separate word, spelled with the tethering rope ṯ, and it comes after the subject or after particles like mk. Check where it stands: glued between the stem and the subject, it is the passive .tw.

blocks.html: .tw is the easiest passive to spot (The sḏm.tw=f Passive), but Middle Egyptian has others, and some of them show no ending at all.

Things done to someone can be said with (1) the sḏm.tw=f, (2) the passive sḏm=f, which looks like an ordinary sḏm=f, (3) the stative of a transitive verb (jw pr ḫtm.w "the house is sealed"), and (4) a passive participle (mrj nb=f "beloved of his lord").

The passive sḏm=f had its own vowels, and sometimes a w ending that scribes now and then wrote. Since both were usually hidden, it looks just like the active sḏm=f. Readers recognize it by sense: rdj n=j t cannot mean "he gives me bread", because nobody is named as the giver; it means "bread was given to me". The passive sḏm=f is the usual passive for past events, as in narrative.

blocks.html: A practical order when a sentence seems to have no doer: first look for .tw; then check whether the subject stands before the verb with a stative ending; then whether the verb describes a noun like an adjective. If none of these fits and the sense still calls for a passive, you are probably looking at a passive sḏm=f. Grammars disagree on how many passive forms there are and what to call them; the meanings, though, are clear from context.

blocks.html: You know the sḏm=f (What the sḏm=f Means) and the sḏm.n=f (What the sḏm.n=f Means). Put the negative n "not" in front of them and something surprising happens.
n sḏm=f means "he did not hear", a past. n sḏm.n=f means "he cannot hear" or "he does not hear", a present or general statement. The two forms seem to swap their meanings when negated.

The swap is less strange than it looks. The n negates a whole statement, and the forms after it are not quite the positive sḏm=f and sḏm.n=f you know. "He did not hear" denies that a hearing ever took place, so Egyptian used the form that names the act itself. "He cannot hear" denies that he has ever achieved hearing, a completed result, so it used the form of completion. Whatever the history, Gardiner's rule holds in practice: read n sḏm=f as a past, n sḏm.n=f as "cannot" or "does not".

blocks.html: The second negative, nn, is the n of Negation with n with one more n. It has two main jobs.
nn + a noun means "there is no …": nn mw "there is no water", nn zꜣ=f "he has no son" (there is no son of his). nn + a sḏm=f negates the future: nn sḏm=f "he will not hear".

Saying that something does not exist is a basic kind of negation, and many languages have a separate word for it (English "there is no", French "il n'y a pas"). Egyptian uses nn. The positive counterpart is wn "exist" or a plain adverbial sentence; nn wn mw "there is no water" puts the two together. For verbs, nn with the sḏm=f denies something that is expected or promised: "he will not hear", "I will not tell a lie".

blocks.html: Middle Egyptian has a second nn, the demonstrative "these, this" from This and That. It is followed by the genitive n and a noun: nn n rmṯ "these people" (literally "these of people"); alone it means "this": ḏd.n=f nn "he said this".
Keep the three negatives apart by what comes after them: n + a verb form for past and present, nn + a sḏm=f for the future, nn + a noun for "there is no".

Confusing nn "there is no" with nn "these". Look at what follows. The negative nn is followed directly by a noun, by wn, or by a sḏm=f; the demonstrative nn is followed by the genitive n and a noun, or stands alone as an object. In hieroglyphs they are also spelled differently: the negative with the arms sign, the demonstrative with water signs only.

blocks.html: One verb form is so tied to two little words that it is learned with them. It looks like the sḏm=f with a t, and so it is called the sḏmt=f.
The sḏmt=f follows n or r: n sḏmt=f means "he has not yet heard" (in a story, "before he heard"); r sḏmt=f means "until he hears".

Both uses look forward to an event that has not happened at the moment spoken of. "He has not yet heard" and "until he hears" point at the same future hearing, one from the side of "not yet", the other from "up to the time". The t marks a form specialized for such not-yet-happened events. It is rare outside these phrases, and a few others like m-ḫt sḏmt=f "after he has heard".

blocks.html: In a narrative, n sḏmt=f is often best translated "before": "before his messenger had come" rather than "his messenger has not yet come". The Egyptian says the second; good English often prefers the first.

The sḏmt=f of weak verbs follows the class rules you know: third-weak verbs use their short stem, jrt=f from jrj, and jj "come" gives jjt=f. That makes r jrt=k "until you do" look like the infinitive jrt with a suffix, and indeed the two are hard to tell apart in writing. The word before it, n or r, and the sense of "not yet" or "until" tell you it is the sḏmt=f.

blocks.html: The negatives n and nn stand at the head of a clause (Negation with n, nn, "There Is No"). Some forms cannot take them: an infinitive after a preposition, a participle describing a noun, a verb after jr "if". For these Egyptian has a negative verb.

tm "not to do" negates forms that cannot take n: infinitives (r tm sḏm "so as not to hear"), participles (tm sḏm "one who does not hear") and verbs after jr or rdj (jr tm=k sḏm "if you do not listen"). tm takes the form the sentence needs, and the verb after it carries the meaning.

tm is a verb meaning "stop, not do". It can be an infinitive, a participle or a sḏm=f like any other verb, so it slips into places where n cannot go. The verb after it is in a special form Gardiner calls the negatival complement, often written with -w: tm=f sḏm(w). In transliteration many books leave the w in brackets or out.

blocks.html: Commands come in The Imperative: sḏm "listen!". The negative command, "do not listen!", needs a word of its own.
A negative command uses m "do not!", the command form of the negative verb jmj, followed by the verb: m sḏm "do not listen!", m ḏd grg "do not tell lies!", m jr ḏwt "do not do evil!".

m works like tm (The Negative Verb tm): it is a negative verb, here in its imperative, and the verb after it says what is not to be done. That verb is in the negatival complement, sometimes written with -w (m sḏmw). Wisdom texts are full of such commands, since they teach what to avoid.

blocks.html: In hieroglyphs the negative m is usually written with the owl and the sign of two outstretched arms, the same gesture used for n. The plain preposition m has no such sign. When you read transliteration only, as in this lesson, the word after m decides.

A famous line from the Eloquent Peasant uses this pattern several times in a row, as the peasant lectures the official: do not lie, do not be light, do not speak falsely. Lines like these, built on m + verb, are some of the easiest sentences in Middle Egyptian literature to read, and among the most quoted.

blocks.html: So far most sentences have been single clauses. Real texts chain clauses together, and Egyptian often does it without any word like "when" or "while".

A clause placed after a main clause, with no word to introduce it, often describes the circumstances of the main clause. Translate it with "when", "while", "as" or an "-ing" word: gm.n=j sw sḏr.w "I found him lying down"; ḏd.n=f n=j jw=j m pr "he spoke to me while I was in the house".

English joins clauses with conjunctions; Egyptian often lets the order speak. A main clause tells what happened (gm.n=j sw "I found him"), and a following clause with a stative, a pseudoverbal phrase, or jw + an adverbial sentence tells the situation at that moment. Gardiner calls these circumstantial clauses. The stative and the jw-clause are the commonest ways to build them, because both describe states.

blocks.html: Which English word to use depends on the sense: "while" for something going on, "when" for a moment, "as" for both, "-ing" for a short description, and sometimes "although" or "since". Egyptian leaves that choice to the reader, so translations of the same passage can differ here without either being wrong.

Translating every clause as a separate sentence. "I found him. He lay down." turns one scene into two events and loses the point that he was already lying there. Check: if a clause after a main verb has a stative, a ḥr + infinitive, or jw + an adverbial phrase, try joining it with "while", "when" or "-ing".

blocks.html: You have met jr as the verb "do" and as the first word of jr sḏm.n=k "if you have heard" (What the sḏm.n=f Means). The second jr is a particle, and it is the main way to say "if".
The particle jr "if" introduces a condition, usually with a sḏm=f or a sḏm.n=f: jr sḏm=k "if you listen", jr sḏm.n=k "if you have heard". Before a noun it means "as for": jr z pn "as for this man".

"If" and "as for" do the same work: they set something up first and then say something about it. "As for this man, he…" sets up a person; "if you listen, you…" sets up a situation. So it is not surprising that one particle does both. The main clause follows, often a sḏm=f or a command: jr sḏm=k mdt=j … "if you listen to my words, …".

Reading jr as the verb "do" at the head of a clause. "Do your hearing" for jr sḏm=k makes no sense of the sentence. Check where it stands and what follows: a jr that opens a clause and is followed by a verb form is "if"; followed by a noun it is "as for". The verb "do" is usually spelled with the eye; the particle with the reed leaf and the mouth.

blocks.html: A clause can also tell why something was done: "he came to see the god", "he gave me bread so that I might live". Egyptian has two common ways to say this.

Purpose is shown with r + infinitive, "in order to": jj.n=j r mꜣꜣ nfrw=k "I have come to see your beauty"; or with a sḏm=f right after another verb, "so that": rdj.n=f n=j t ꜥnḫ=j "he gave me bread so that I might live".

r means "to, toward". Toward a place it means motion; toward an action, the infinitive, it means aim: "toward seeing" is "in order to see". The second way uses a sḏm=f of the kind that expresses wishes and what should happen (What the sḏm=f Means). Placed after a main clause, "he gave me bread, (that) I might live", it gives the intended result.

blocks.html: Purpose clauses with a sḏm=f look like circumstantial clauses (Circumstantial Clauses); the difference is in the sense. A circumstance describes what is already so; a purpose looks ahead to what the action is meant to bring about. Ask whether the second clause is the goal of the first.

Reading r + infinitive as a direction, "toward". "I came toward your beauty, seeing" keeps the words but loses the meaning. Check: if r is followed by an infinitive after a verb of motion or action, translate "in order to" or "to".

blocks.html: A preposition with an infinitive, ḥr sḏm "on hearing" (Using the Infinitive), can follow a subject just as a place phrase does in the adverbial sentence. The result works like a verb tense, and Gardiner named it the pseudo-verbal construction.

Subject + ḥr + infinitive means "is doing": jw=f ḥr sḏm "he is hearing". Subject + r + infinitive means "is going to do, will do": jw=f r sḏm "he will hear". With verbs of motion, subject + m + infinitive means "is going, is coming": jw nsw m jjt "the king is coming".

The sentence is built like z m pr "the man is in the house": a subject and a prepositional phrase. Only the phrase is now an action. "He is on hearing" means he is in the middle of it; "he is toward hearing" means it lies ahead; "he is in coming" means he is on his way. English uses "is …ing" and "will" for the same ideas; old English even said "he is a-coming", with a preposition.

blocks.html: Like the stative, this construction needs a subject in front, so it appears after jw or mk, after a noun, and in circumstantial clauses: sḏm.n=j ḫrw=f jw=f ḥr mdt "I heard his voice as he was speaking" (Circumstantial Clauses). In later Egyptian it grew into the main present tense of the language.

Reading ḥr here as "on" or "upon". "He is on the hearing" is the literal meaning, but the sense is "he is hearing". Check: if ḥr, r or m is followed by an infinitive, and a subject stands before them, translate as a verb: "is doing", "will do", "is going".

blocks.html: ntj introduces a relative clause after a noun like "the man" (The Relative Adjective ntj). After "a man" Egyptian often does without it.

After an indefinite noun ("a man", "a town"), a plain clause can describe the noun with no ntj: z ḏd=f mꜣꜥt "a man who speaks the truth"; njwt n rḫ=j rn=s "a town whose name I do not know". A pronoun in the clause points back to the noun.

A definite noun is already known, so the relative clause picks out which one: "the man who is in the house". An indefinite noun is new, and the clause after it simply adds a description, the way a circumstantial clause adds circumstances. Egyptian treats it that way: no special word, just a clause with a pronoun (=f, =s, =sn) that refers back. Gardiner calls these virtual relative clauses, relative in sense without a relative word.

blocks.html: Because Egyptian has no word for "the" or "a", the line between definite and indefinite is not always visible. Use the sense of the passage: a person or place introduced for the first time is usually indefinite, and a clause right after it, with a pronoun pointing back, is likely a virtual relative.

Looking for ntj in every relative clause, and reading z ḏd=f mꜣꜥt as two statements, "a man; he speaks the truth". Check: after a noun, does the next clause have a pronoun that refers back to it? Then it probably describes the noun: "who…", "whose…".

blocks.html: This lesson is different from the others. It does not teach a settled rule; it shows a question that Egyptologists have argued about for decades, and how to read texts while the argument goes on.

Some sentences seem to stress an adverbial part (a place, time, manner or purpose) rather than the verb: jj.n=j m njwt=j can be "I came from my town" or "it was from my town that I came". Scholars debate whether special emphatic verb forms mark this stress, how many there are, and what to call them.

Hieroglyphs hide vowels, and some verb forms that looked the same in writing probably sounded different. In Coptic, the last stage of the language, special "second tenses" put the stress on an adverbial phrase. H. J. Polotsky argued that Middle Egyptian had such forms too, among the sḏm=f and sḏm.n=f, and his view (often called the Standard Theory) shaped Egyptian grammar for a generation. Later scholars refined or challenged it. Some grammars, such as Allen's, speak of nominal forms; others prefer to describe stress through context alone. Gardiner's grammar of 1927 predates the debate and describes these forms in other terms.

For the reader: most grammars agree that some sentences put the weight on an adverbial phrase, and that context is the best guide to when.

blocks.html: Every verb form so far has had a subject, named or understood. The imperative, the command form, speaks to its subject directly, so it has none.

The imperative is usually the bare stem: sḏm "hear! listen!", ḏd "say!", jr "do!" (from jrj). Two common verbs use special words: jmj "give!" (for rdj) and mj "come!" (for jj). jnj "bring" has jn "bring!".

A command is said to someone who is there, so "you" goes without saying, in Egyptian as in English ("Listen!", not "You listen!"). Third-weak verbs drop their j, as in most forms. The special words for "give!" and "come!" are old forms that survived because these commands were used so often, much as English uses "go!" but says "went" in the past.

blocks.html: When a command is given to several people, scribes sometimes add the -w of the plural or three plural strokes; in transliteration it is often left out. Commands can also be softened or strengthened with particles and a reflexive phrase, like n=k "for yourself", which you will meet in reading but can translate loosely or not at all.
A command can be followed by a sḏm=f: jmj sḏm=f "let him hear" (rdj with the sḏm=f). For a negative command, Egyptian uses m (Do Not!).

blocks.html: Commands are common in wisdom texts, letters and the speeches of stories. In the Eloquent Peasant, the peasant's pleas to the high steward are full of them, and in letters a writer often closes with a command to the reader: "write to me about it", "take care of it". Spotting the bare stem at the head of a clause is the key.

Adding a suffix pronoun to a command. sḏm=k is not "listen!" but "you listen" or "may you listen", a sḏm=f. The imperative has no suffix: sḏm. Check: if the verb has a suffix pronoun, it is not an imperative.

blocks.html: A statement becomes a question in Egyptian by putting a word in front of it, or by putting a question word where the answer would go.

jn (or jn jw) at the head of a sentence asks a yes-or-no question: jn jw=k m pr "are you in the house?", jn sḏm.n=k "have you heard?". Question words stand where the answer would be: zj "who? what?", jḫ "what?", ptr "what? who?", tnj "where?": zj pw "who is it?", jw=k tnj "where are you?".

Many languages mark yes-or-no questions with a word at the front (French "est-ce que", Latin "-ne"). Egyptian uses jn. A question word, on the other hand, replaces the missing piece: in jw=k m pr "you are in the house" the place is m pr; in jw=k tnj "where are you?" tnj takes its slot. In zj pw "who is it?", zj takes the place of a noun in a pw sentence (Sentences with pw).

blocks.html: You know jw and mk from jw and mk. They belong to a family of small words, particles, that do not change the facts of a sentence but its tone or its place in a story.

Learn these first: mk "look, behold" (points to what follows), jsṯ "now, meanwhile" (sets a scene), ḥꜣ "would that, if only" (a wish), jn (asks a question) and jr "if, as for" (sets up a condition or topic). Many more exist; translate them by their effect, not word for word.

English does the same with "well", "now", "look", "oh". They are hard to translate one by one, but they guide a listener. Egyptian particles split into two groups: those that stand at the head of a sentence, like mk, jsṯ and ḥꜣ, and "enclitic" ones that lean on the first word, like js, grt and ḥm. Gardiner gives each group a lesson of its own.

blocks.html: Among the enclitic particles, js has several uses: it can mark a clause as dependent ("as", "since"), and with n before a word it negates just that word, "it is not … that". Others, like grt and ḥm, add emphasis or mark the next step of an argument, and English often shows them with punctuation, word order or nothing at all.

Translating each particle literally. "Behold, now, would that" in every line makes a translation stiff and strange. Many particles are best shown with tone, a dash, an exclamation mark, or left out. Check: does your English sound like something a person would say? Particles should help it, not clutter it.

blocks.html: jn asks questions (Questions) and means "by". Before a noun and a participle it has a third job: it points at the doer.

jn + noun + participle means "it is (noun) who does": jn nsw rdj ḥtp "it is the king who gives an offering". With a sḏm=f instead of a participle it refers to the future: jn nsw rdj=f n=k t "it is the king who will give you bread".

English singles out a doer with a "cleft" sentence: not "the king gives", but "it is the king who gives". Egyptian builds the same thing from pieces you know. The participle names the action ("one who gives", Active Participles), the noun names the doer, and jn marks the noun as the one meant, probably from its sense "by": "by the king (is) the giving". With a pronoun instead of a noun, Egyptian uses an independent pronoun (Independent Pronouns): ntf sḏm "it is he who hears".

blocks.html: A Middle Kingdom stela is a slab of stone, usually round-topped, set up in a tomb chapel or at a holy place like Abydos. Thousands survive, and most follow one plan. You already know its opening from The Offering Formula and its list of gifts from Bread, Beer and the Voice Offering. Now read it as a whole.

A stela's text usually runs: (1) the formula ḥtp-dj-nsw "an offering that the king gives"; (2) the god or gods, with their titles; (3) the gifts, dj=f prt-ḫrw t ḥnqt kꜣ ꜣpd… "that he may give an invocation offering of bread and beer, oxen and fowl…"; (4) n kꜣ n "for the ka of" the owner, with his titles and name, often ending mꜣꜥ-ḫrw "true of voice".

The stela is a request that never expires. The king, in theory the only one who could make offerings to the gods, gives an offering; the god passes its benefit on to the dead; and anyone who reads the text aloud makes the "invocation offering" (prt-ḫrw, literally "going out of the voice") real again. That is why the gifts are listed so carefully, and why the owner's name must be there: the offering is for that ka and no other.

blocks.html: Many stelae name not only their owner but his family: parents, wife, children, sometimes servants. The phrases are few and fixed, and they use grammar you now know: participles (Passive Participles) and relative forms (Relative Forms).
Family phrases to know: zꜣ=f mrj=f "his beloved son", zꜣt=f mrt=f "his beloved daughter", ḥmt=f mrt=f "his beloved wife", nbt-pr "lady of the house", and ms.n or jr.n + a woman's name, "born of …".

mrj=f is a passive participle with a suffix, "beloved of him", so zꜣ=f mrj=f is "his son, his beloved one". ms.n is a relative form of msj "give birth": "whom (she) bore". The mother's name follows as the subject: ms.n nbt-pr nfrt "whom the lady of the house Nefret bore", that is, "born of the lady of the house Nefret". jr.n, "whom (she) made", says the same thing. Egyptians traced people through their mothers on these monuments as a matter of course.

blocks.html: From the Old Kingdom on, officials carved accounts of their lives on tomb walls and stelae. They are called autobiographies, though they follow conventions as fixed as those of the offering formula. Their grammar is the jw + sḏm.n=f of jw sḏm.n=f in Narrative, line after line.

A set phrase of many autobiographies: jw rdj.n=j t n ḥqr ḥbs n ḥꜣy "I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked". Others: ḏd.n=j mꜣꜥt jr.n=j mꜣꜥt "I spoke what is right and did what is right". These are ideal statements of a good life, not personal confessions.

A tomb was a public place. Visitors were asked to read the offering formula aloud for the owner, and the owner's claim to deserve it was his life lived by maat, right order. So he set down the deeds that maat required: feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, speaking truly, harming no one. Because every good official claimed the same virtues, the same phrases recur from tomb to tomb. Some autobiographies add real events too, such as journeys and royal favors; Harkhuf of Aswan, for example, describes his expeditions to the south.

blocks.html: The Tale of Sinuhe is the most admired work of Middle Egyptian literature. It was composed in the early 12th Dynasty, in the Middle Kingdom, and was still copied by scribes centuries later. It is told in the first person, like a tomb autobiography (Tomb Autobiographies), and it opens the same way.

The tale begins with the hero's titles, then his name and ḏd=f "he says": zꜣ-nht ḏd=f "Sinuhe says". Then comes a date, ḥꜣt-zp 30 ꜣbd 3 ꜣḫt sw 7 "Year 30, third month of the Flood season, day 7", and the news that sets the story moving: ꜥr nṯr r ꜣḫt=f "the god ascended to his horizon", that is, King Amenemhat I died.

Opening with titles told an Egyptian reader at once what kind of text this was: the life of an official, set down in his own voice. The date follows the usual pattern of Writing a Date, counted from the start of the king's reign. And the king's death is told in the polite language of royal texts: the king is nṯr "the god", and he does not die, he "ascends to his horizon", the place where the sun rises and sets.

blocks.html: At that moment the king's son, the future Senusret I, was away leading an army against the Libyans, and Sinuhe was with the expedition. What he overhears there drives the rest of the story (Sinuhe: The Flight). Whether the old king died naturally or in a palace plot is not said in the tale; another text, the Teaching of Amenemhat, speaks of an attack on him, and scholars discuss how the two relate.

Expecting the hero's name first. Students look for "Sinuhe" at the start and are puzzled by a string of titles (the tale opens jrj-pꜥt ḥꜣtj-ꜥ "hereditary noble and count" and more). Check: in an autobiographical text, titles come first, then the name, then ḏd=f "he says".

blocks.html: In the camp in Libya, Sinuhe overhears messengers bringing the news of the king's death to the prince. His reaction is the most vivid scene of the tale, and the journey that follows crosses half the map of the Near East.

Sinuhe panics and flees: through the Delta, past the border forts called the Walls of the Ruler, across the desert where he nearly dies of thirst, to Byblos and then Qedem, and finally to Upper Retjenu, where the ruler Amunenshi welcomes him: nfr tw ḥnꜥ=j sḏm=k r n kmt "you will fare well with me; you will hear the speech of Egypt".

The tale never fully explains why he ran. He says his heart failed him; he later insists to the new king that it was like a dream. Many readers think the vagueness is the point: a loyal official, caught in a moment of terror, acts against everything his upbringing taught him and spends the rest of the story finding his way back to Egypt and to a proper burial.

blocks.html: The flight is told with quick verbs, many of them sḏm.n=f forms with =j: he hides in a bush, crosses water at night, passes the forts, and walks until he collapses with thirst. A sheikh of the herdsmen, who had been in Egypt and recognized him, gives him water and boiled milk. That act of kindness turns the story from flight to a new life abroad.

Losing track of who is speaking. The narrative is Sinuhe's, but it quotes others, such as Amunenshi, who speak to Sinuhe as =k "you". Check: mark every =j as Sinuhe in the narrative; when a speech begins (often after ḏd.n=f or ḏd.jn=f "then he said"), switch to the speaker's point of view.

blocks.html: The Tale of the Eloquent Peasant was composed in the Middle Kingdom and set in an earlier time, under a king Nebkaure of Herakleopolis. It is part story and part showcase of fine speech, and it opens with the classic first line of an Egyptian tale.

z pw wn ḫw-n-jnpw rn=f "There was a man named Khun-Anup"; sḫtj pw n sḫt-ḥmꜣt "he was a peasant of the Field of Salt". Robbed of his donkeys on the way to market, he pleads with the high steward Rensi in nine speeches, full of praise, complaint and irony: jr mꜣꜥt n nb mꜣꜥt "Do what is right for the lord of what is right!".

The story asks what justice means when the powerful ignore the weak. The thief, Nemtynakht, is a servant of Rensi's estate; the peasant has only his words. The king, delighted by his eloquence, orders Rensi to keep silent so that the peasant will go on speaking, to have the speeches written down, and to see that the peasant's family is fed meanwhile. The tale ends with justice done and the thief's goods given to the peasant. Readers then and now enjoy the speeches as both art and argument.

blocks.html: The speeches use every tool of the language: commands, negative commands (m + verb), conditions with jr, and long chains of epithets. In the speeches the peasant calls Rensi the rudder and the balance of justice, and then accuses him of steering crooked and weighing falsely.

Taking the peasant's praise of the official at face value. He calls Rensi "father of the orphan, husband of the widow", then complains that the balance is crooked and the judge corrupt. The speeches mix praise, complaint and irony on purpose. Check: read each image together with the reproach that follows it.

blocks.html: The Rosetta Stone carries one decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs at the top, Demotic in the middle and Greek at the bottom. It was issued by an assembly of priests at Memphis in 196 BC, in the reign of Ptolemy V, and its hieroglyphic text is the part you can now begin to read.

The hieroglyphic text names the king in cartouches, most often ptwlmys ꜥnḫ ḏt mrj ptḥ "Ptolemy, living forever, beloved of Ptah". It ends by ordering the decree to be written m sẖ n mdw-nṯr sẖ n šꜥt sẖ n ḥꜣw-nbw "in the writing of the god's words (hieroglyphs), the writing of documents (Demotic) and the writing of the Greeks".

The language of the hieroglyphic text is the traditional one of temple inscriptions, close to Middle Egyptian, but the scribes wrote it well over a thousand years after the Middle Kingdom. Their spellings and some of their signs are those of the Ptolemaic Period, and a few constructions reflect later stages of Egyptian. So you will recognize much of the grammar and many words, and you should expect late spellings rather than the classical ones of Sinuhe.

blocks.html: You can now parse most of a Middle Egyptian sentence: find the verb, name its form, find its subject and object. The last step is to turn that analysis into English that a reader would want to read.

A good translation keeps the meaning and the tone, not the word order. jw=j jj.kj is not "is I come-I" but "I have come"; zꜣ=f mrj=f is not "his son, his beloved" but "his beloved son"; z pw wn… is "there was once a man…".

Every language packs meaning differently. Egyptian puts the verb first, uses jw and mk where English uses nothing or "look", leaves out "is", and chains clauses with no conjunctions. A word-for-word gloss is useful to check your parsing, but it is not a translation. The goal is English that says what the Egyptian says, with nothing added and nothing lost, in the way an English speaker would say it.

blocks.html: Two more habits help. Translate the time last: decide what the form means (completed, general, wished, a state) before choosing an English tense. And read a whole passage before polishing a single sentence, since particles, circumstantial clauses and quoted speech all depend on what comes around them.

Translating word for word. "Is I come-I" keeps every word and loses the sentence. Check by reading your English aloud: if no English speaker would say it, go back to the parse and say the same meaning naturally. Then check the other way: does your smooth English still match every form you parsed?

blocks.html: When you meet a sign you do not know, you need to find it. Gardiner's sign list, the last part of his Egyptian Grammar, is the standard tool, and its codes are the ones this course has used all along (Common Determinatives).

Gardiner's list sorts signs by what they show into lettered groups: A man, B woman, C gods in human form, D parts of the human body, E mammals, F parts of mammals, G birds, H parts of birds, I reptiles and amphibians, K fish, L insects and small animals, M plants, N sky, earth and water, O buildings, P ships, Q furniture, R temple furniture, S crowns and dress, T weapons, U tools, V rope and baskets, W vessels, X bread, Y writing and games, Z strokes, Aa unclassified. Each sign has a number in its group: G1 is the vulture.

A beginner who meets a sign cannot look it up by sound, since its sound is what is unknown, nor by meaning, since that depends on how it is used. What anyone can see is the picture. So Gardiner arranged the list by picture, group by group, and gave each sign its uses: sound values, word-sign meanings, determinative uses. There is no group J; Gardiner left it out.

blocks.html: Once you can read a word's consonants, you can look it up. Middle Egyptian dictionaries are ordered by transliteration, in the alphabet you learned in Transliteration and Its Order.

Dictionaries list words in the order ꜣ j y ꜥ w b p f m n r h ḥ ḫ ẖ z s š q k g t ṯ d ḏ, letter by letter. Look up the base word: a verb under its full root (jr.n=f under jrj), a noun under its singular masculine form (nṯrw under nṯr), an adjective under its masculine (nfrt under nfr).

A dictionary cannot list every form of every word; it lists each word once, under a headword. For verbs that means the root, with weak consonants put back, since those are what change from form to form. Endings like .n, .tw, -t, -w and suffix pronouns belong to the grammar, not the dictionary. So before you look a word up, strip it down: take off suffixes and endings, restore any weak j, and you have the headword.
